“There can be no doubt whatsoever, Charlie, this is an election which everyone who was there will never forget.”

Good Morning America is playing on your TV at your HQ in Austin, where you spent a restless night not knowing whether your long, hard-fought quest would succeed. Now, as you pour yourself a morning cup of coffee, your morning ritual, you can hear the anchors, Diane Sawyer and Charlie Gibson, discussing the events of last night. Cecile already broke the news to you over the phone a few minutes ago. In fact, that’s why you turned on the TV in the first place. A part of you had been dreading to even look, out of some arcane superstition. You didn’t want to find out from anyone else.

You look on as the co-anchors continue to talk about the results of last night’s election while a map is shown on the screen. The states that voted for you are colored blue, Thompson’s are red. Below the map is the final tally. And it’s at that moment that it really hits you. It’s at that moment that it starts to sink in. You, Ann Richards, former Governor of Texas, current Vice-President of the United States, have been elected the 43rd President of the United States.

This was the textbook close election. You and Fred Thompson traded blows, the polls remained razor thin in the final weeks, and many pundits soon gave up on even trying to predict the outcome. The country had become a battleground upon which the course of America in the new millennium would be decided, and as you poured your entire heart and soul into the campaign, a part of you worried that it might not be enough.

Now, you feel all of those fears and anxieties wash away. You have followed in the footsteps of LBJ and will bring your Democratic Texan flair to Washington, and you’ve also made history. You are the first woman ever elected to the highest office in the land. This is a monumental achievement that will live on in the memory long after you are gone. Our young women will truly know they can be anything now, even President; the glass ceiling has finally been shattered.

As for what comes next, that depends on how well you can work with Congress. The good news is Democrats have held on to the Senate majority. We even got Jim Jeffords to change parties. The bad news is that despite some gains, the House is still under narrow GOP control, so you can expect Denny Hastert and his gang to shut down most of our attempts at legislation. However, after your historic victory, there will be pressure to collaborate for the good of the nation.

You watch the show for a while longer, just basking in the glow of it all while Charlie and Diane discuss exactly what this result means for us on a political and human level. You soon receive a call from President Cuomo to congratulate you. He’s an amazing man and will be a tough act to follow, but there’s a reason he chose you in ‘92: he knew that if anyone could carry the torch, it was you. It is now up to you whether you will continue Cuomo’s quest to return the Democrats to the golden age of FDR, or take a different course, one uniquely your own.

As for the Republicans, three straight defeats will have them re-evaluating and recalculating. It’s anyone’s guess who they’ll put up in ‘04. But right now, you don’t care. It's been one hell of a year, and there’s a long road ahead, so you deserve at least a short time to yourself before giving your victory speech to your overjoyed supporters. Get plenty of rest, Madam VP, and by the by, you might want to get used to being called Madam President.

“For those who have stayed with us, we do have a major projection: Vice-President Richards has just secured a historic victory…”

You had been one of those brave souls who kept watching NBC’s election night broadcast late into the night. You knew you wouldn’t have been able to sleep without knowing. And so you held back your exhaustion and pressed on, hanging on Tom Brokaw’s every word. Then came the projection, the one that finally released all the tension that had built up your campaign HQ. You had done it. You had pushed yourself to the limit for weeks, months, never really knowing if the American people were listening to your message. The polls were razor thin, and almost everyone agreed the race was a toss up, but you never took a single vote for granted.

After all, despite running to succeed a relatively popular incumbent, you faced numerous challenges to reach this point. After eight years of liberalism, there was fear amongst your camp that the country would naturally swing to the right. You had to unite the party after a tough primary battle. And perhaps the greatest hurdle you had to overcome, the one thing you can’t control: your sex.

You are a woman in what was once thought to be a man’s world. Many naysayers said it could never happen, but you never paid them any mind, and now you have proven them all wrong. Women all across America, and the men who have loyally stood by them, will wake up to a new world, one with a woman elected to the highest office in the land..

You exchange weary, but elated smiles, laughter, and hugs with everyone; you could never have completed this long and arduous journey without their support. They have been there in your lowest moments, and they have given you advice and counsel throughout each step of this campaign. The next morning, you will receive the concession call from Fred Thompson, which you will graciously accept. He was a tough opponent; the two of you battled for the course of America’s future in the new millennium, and some experts thought that 2000 might be a bridge too far for the governing party. However, your message clearly began to resonate as the weeks went on. In the end, your actions and words inspired the nation to give the Democrats another four years to enact their agenda, with you at the helm.

You will follow in the footsteps of LBJ and bring your unique Texan flair to Washington, but what happens next will depend on you and how well you can work with Congress. Democrats are still the minority in the House of Representatives despite some small gains, meaning Hastert will do everything in his power to block our legislation. On the other hand, we managed to hold on to our Senate majority, and even gain a seat thanks to Jim Jeffords switching parties. In any event, after your strong performance and historic achievement, there will be pressure on the Republicans to work with us in the first year for the good of the nation.

You watch the results come in for a while longer as Brokaw and Tim Russert talk about what this means for America, not only on a political level, but a human one. Your victory has truly opened the door for millions of young women across the country, who will now know that nothing, even being President, is beyond their reach; the glass ceiling has finally been shattered.

You receive another call, this one from President Cuomo to congratulate you. He really is an amazing man, and will be a tough act to follow, but there’s a reason he chose you in ‘92: he knew that if anyone could carry the torch, it was you. And thus it will fall to you to decide whether to continue to take the Democratic Party back to the golden age of FDR, or chart a course that is uniquely your own.

As for the Republicans, three straight defeats will have them re-evaluating and recalculating. It’s anyone’s guess who they’ll put up in ‘04. But right now, you aren’t particularly bothered. You have a few hours to get some much-needed sleep and prepare a victory address for your supporters; the nation is waiting to see just what kind of leader Dorothy Ann Richards will be. So get plenty of rest, Madam VP, and by the by, you might want to get used to being called Madam President.

“It has been a historic election, and we here at NBC can now project a historic result: Vice-President Ann Richards has secured the Presidency with a significant mandate.”

The mood at your HQ in Austin had been cautiously celebratory as the polls began to close. Your staffers and Cecile were confident that you had done enough to win. You know that you had too, but you still had to see it to believe it. When Tom Brokaw said this early in the election night broadcast, you immediately felt a plethora of emotions.

Joy, relief, satisfaction, and a deep sense of reverence and understanding of what it took to get here. Your team embraces you, there is smiling and laughter. Cecile is as proud as a daughter ever could be, and she is far from the only one. Your run was not just for yourself, it was for a dream over a century in the making, the dream of reaffirming America’s commitment to being the land of opportunity for all.

You faced many potential obstacles in this election; a party divided between its left and center, the natural voter fatigue that sets in after an eight year presidency, and the one issue many pundits had said might cause your downfall: your sex. The naysayers said America would not vote for a woman president, but you went out there as only you can and resoundingly proved them wrong with a Texas-sized landslide. Women all across America, and the men who have loyally stood by them, are united in their joy at this watershed moment in American history.

The moment still seems surreal to you as you take a victory lap at HQ. Some of the most heartfelt moments are with your young interns. They’re giddy with the taste of success, many of them are still in high school or college, and this will become a lifelong memory for them. A reminder that for all the toils of politics, there are moments like this, moments where the country unites for a greater purpose. Fred Thompson calls to concede, which you graciously accept.

Democrats have managed to erase the Republican gains of two years ago, regaining control of the House, which means Gephardt will take the gavel and be receptive to your agenda. \";\nrichardsWinLand = \"

“Tonight, we honor the legacy of Dorothy Ann Richards, a one of a kind president…”

(What follows is a transcript from an NBC special report on the passing of President Richards)

Former President Ann Richards passed away today, September 13th, 2006, at her home in Austin, Texas, after a lengthy battle with esophageal cancer. The outpouring of grief from the country has been tremendous. To her supporters, Ms. Richards seemed practically immortal. Her clever wit and homespun charm never faded, even when she was in her final days. According to her family, she kept responding to letters from devotees until she was physically unable, then had others write them for her. Now; the nation is just beginning to come to terms with the loss.

And yet, mixed in with the sadness of this moment are also joy and pride. Today, supporters in all fifty states have organized events to celebrate the life of an American icon. Ms. Richards lived a full life, serving her home state of Texas as Governor, then the nation with President Cuomo as his Vice-President in the 1990s, but it was after her landslide election to the Presidency in 2000, a watershed moment for this country - the first ever female president - that she fully came into her own.

Ms. Richards brought her Texas charm to the Oval Office, but she also brought a heartfelt commitment to building on the legacy of President Cuomo and addressing the issues of women’s rights and education, which she had spent her entire career fighting for. In just four years, with a united Congress behind her, President Richards oversaw the passage of the Paycheck Fairness Act, a law codifying abortion rights, and comprehensive education reform. She also signed a major bipartisan cap-and-trade bill to limit carbon emissions, a significant boost for the environmental movement and considered by many to be a signature accomplishment that will inspire further action to combat global warming.

Many analysts believe President Richards could have won re-election easily, but with her health failing, she made the decision to decline to seek a second term, and spend her final years surrounded by her family and close friends. Regardless of her one-term status, however, the name and legacy of Ann Richards will now be added to the rich tapestry of transformative American leadership...

“Well, Diane, we’ve got a few Ann Richards supporters here with us to talk about their thoughts on last night’s election…”

You’re watching Good Morning America play on the TV set at your HQ in Austin, where you spent a restless night being left in the dark along with the rest of the nation about the outcome of the election. You barely slept. You wanted to stay up, you checked all the major networks, but all of them had the race as too close to call.

Finally, your advisors and Cecile had convinced you to get what fleeting rest you could and to leave the rest to them. You hugged, shook hands and thanked all of them for what they’d done for you; you knew that this campaign could never have gotten off the ground without them, and it was only through their tireless efforts that you stayed in this race to the very end.

Now, it’s over. You take a melancholy sip from your coffee as you watch Diane Sawyer and Charlie Gibson interviewing a small panel of your supporters. The theme from all of them is the same: pride in you and what you stood for, and heartbreak at the outcome. You feel a pang of grief; seeing this now just confirms what Cecile had already told you on the phone a few minutes ago. Despite all of your efforts, all the blood, sweat and tears, the battle was lost.

What hurts the most is just how close it was. You look at the little election map being displayed on the screen. If just one or two states here or there had flipped, the outcome could’ve been completely different. You and Thompson were neck and neck for weeks, and pundits had pretty much given up on trying to predict the outcome, but in the end, there was something about your message that didn’t land.

Or maybe all the doubters were right, and America just wasn’t ready to break that last glass ceiling and elect a female president. Whatever it was, you will go down in history as a “What If”, and your run, while falling tragically short, will still give real hope to women that the wait may not be long. After all, you got tens of millions of votes, and proved that a woman could be a viable national candidate.

In any event, Fred Thompson will now become the 43rd President of the United States, and it is uncertain how much he will roll back the progress we’ve made under you and President Cuomo. He’s made his disdain for the movement conservatives clear, so we can only hope he’ll push back against the far right and act more like a mainstream conservative. The good news is that while Republicans have held on to the House, Democrats are still in control of the Senate, and we even got Jim Jeffords to flip, so we should be able to stop Denny Hastert from ramming his agenda through.

That’s a cold comfort to you, however. Your career is over, and after decades of working for campaigns, running for office in your home state of Texas, and serving as the Vice-President these past eight years, you find it hard to say goodbye to the life you’ve built in politics. You’ve given so much of yourself to the people, become a beloved icon to them. But now, there’s nothing more to give.

You receive a consolation call from President Cuomo, he offers some kind words, which you receive gratefully. The two of you have become good friends these past eight years, and that won’t change after your term ends. You watch the show a while longer, then finally decide to leave and face the world. You’ve got one last speech to give.

“It has been a long, tense night for both campaigns, but we can now project that Fred Thompson has crossed 270 electoral votes…”

Most of America had gone to sleep, but you couldn’t, you just had to find out. You knew you would just lie awake otherwise. Then Tom Brokaw spoke those words, and you felt a deep sense of exhausted disappointment. You and your team had held out hope to the end that it wouldn’t end up like this, but it was not meant to be. Cecile hugs you, some of your staff offer words of comfort and consolation. You have nothing to be ashamed of, they say.

You thank them all for standing by you to the end, exchanging melancholy hugs and handshakes. You and Thompson were neck and neck for almost the entirety of the campaign, the polls went back and forth so many times that the only thing people could agree on was that it was a total toss up. No matter what you tried, no matter what tactic you used, Thompson was always just a step ahead. The road here has been long and difficult, and the cynics might say it was fruitless. But you dare to hope that it won’t be in vain.

You called Thomspon to concede and wish him the best; he was respectful of your gender throughout the campaign, and never discredited you for being a woman. You will go down in history as a “What if”, and as far as many of your supporters are concerned, there’s one reason and one reason only that many refused to vote for you: you were a woman, running for what has long been seen as a man’s office. But perhaps with your run here, and despite this agonizing defeat, you have shown the world that a woman can run, that she can get broad support from across the country, and that she can win. Perhaps in a better political environment, or with a couple more decades of social progress, the glass ceiling may someday be broken.

In any event. Fred Thompson will now become the 43rd president, and it is uncertain how much he will roll back the progress we’ve made under you and President Cuomo. He’s made his disdain for the movement conservatives clear, so we can only hope he’ll push back against the far right and act more like a mainstream conservative. Unfortunately, Republicans have retained control of the House, though Democrats are still in control of the Senate, thanks partly to Jim Jeffords changing parties, so we should be able to hopefully contain the worst of the far right’s agenda.

That’s a cold comfort to you, however. Your career is over, and after decades of working for campaigns, running for office in your home state of Texas, and serving as the Vice-President these past eight years, you find it hard to say goodbye to the life you’ve built in politics. You’ve given so much of yourself to the people, become a beloved icon to them. But now, there’s nothing more to give.

You receive a consolation call from President Cuomo, he offers some kind words, which you receive gratefully. The two of you have become good friends these past eight years, and that won’t change after your term ends. You watch Brokaw and Tim Russert discussing the results a while longer, then finally decide to leave and face the world. You’ve got one last speech to give.

\";\nrichardsLossLand = \"

“A woman ahead of her time”

(What follows is an excerpt from an article written after the 2020 election)

The nomination of Vice-President Ann Richards was a watershed moment for the Democratic Party and the country at-large. It was the first time that any major party had made a woman their candidate for President. Richards, the former Governor of Texas and Vice-President for eight years under President Cuomo, campaigned on a platform that placed women’s rights front and center in the national discourse, hoping to inspire support for her historic candidacy.

In the immediate aftermath, most analysts concluded that this was a blunder on the part of Ms. Richards, and that her vocal support of feminism was a major factor in pushing most social moderates towards then-Senator Fred Thompson. Despite the polls showing a relatively close race after the respective party conventions, Mr. Thompson was able to secure more support from the political center and ultimately won the election by a landslide margin.

Despite this overwhelming defeat, however, Ms. Richards did not give up on her dream of seeing a woman elected President, and neither did her supporters. As the years went on, historians have noted that Ms. Richards’ campaign has had a similar effect to Barry Goldwater’s doomed effort in 1964, which created the modern conservative movement. In much the same way, Ms. Richards would become a martyr-like figure to her devotees - made all the more stark by her passing in 2006 - and the movement only continued to grow at an accelerated pace. Now, the election of President Amy Klobuchar in 2020, twenty years after Richards’ groundbreaking effort, has seen a renewed interest and appreciation of the former Vice-President as a trailblazer who gave the nation a glimpse into its future…

\";\nrichardsNoMajority = \"

No candidate captured an electoral college majority

This has resulted in a most unusual situation, but not one that will benefit you, unfortunately. Fred Thompson will be chosen as the President by the Republican controlled House, while the Democratic Senate will vote for your running mate to be Vice-President.

It is anyone’s guess how on earth this is going to play out, but the nation can expect to be stuck in gridlock for the next four years under one of the most bizarre power sharing situations in living memory.

\";\nwellstoneWinClose = \"

“Good morning America, and in one of the closest races we’ve ever seen, we at last have a winner…”

You went to sleep last night uncertain of your future. Before the polls closed, most of the pundits still expected Thomspon to take it narrowly. After all, he started the campaign with a lead, and seemed to have an advantage with moderates, who were put off by your full-blown support of progressivism. Even when the polls showed the race tightening, many still dismissed you. Maybe deep down, even you had doubts about whether your fellow Americans would elevate you to the highest office in the land.

Early the next morning, you turned on the TV and were greeted by this message from the Good Morning America team of Charlie Gibson and Diane Sawyer. It felt surreal to find out this way, the same way that many people who didn’t stay up were probably finding out. But perhaps it was fitting for you, the humble son of Ukrainian Jewish immigrants and a lifelong public servant - first as a teacher, then a Senator - to learn your electoral fate from a fluffy morning show.

You watch as Diane and Charlie talk to some analysts and interview some voters from both sides. The race was one of the closest in living memory, a true battle where every state and every vote counted. Despite Cuomo leaving office with a good economy and some landmark achievements, you still had a mountain to climb due to the nation seemingly tiring of big government liberalism and preparing to swing back to the right. You were an underdog in the primaries to begin with, and uniting the party was seen as too tall of a task, let alone uniting the country.

Yet somehow, you managed to pull it off. Whether it was your force of personality, your dogged determination, or perhaps, an underestimation of liberalism’s popularity, you’ve shocked the world again and secured a third consecutive Democratic term. You will now join a proud lineage that stretches from FDR to Mario Cuomo, and will now include you, Paul David Wellstone, the 43rd President of the United States.

You receive a call from Cuomo, congratulating you and wishing you all the best. He will be a valuable counsel to you, just as you were to him. The reality is that your uphill battle won’t end now that you’ve become President. Despite Democrats holding on to their Senate Majority - helped by Jim Jeffords switching parties, Republicans have managed to retain their lead in the House, which means you’ll have to deal with at least two years of Dennis Hastert blocking practically all of your legislation.

You’ve never let the odds begin stacked against you slow you down before though. It’s unknown how much you can get done in your first term, but there’ll be some pressure for the Republicans to cooperate for at least the first few months. If you play your cards right, you can run for re-election in 2004 and try to win four consecutive terms for the Democrats. Then it really will be like the good old days of FDR. None of those thoughts are in your head now though as you continue to watch the show and simply enjoy the relief of the long and grueling campaign finally being over. Your wife Sheila joins you, and you take her hand in yours. You’ll need her support these next four years, it’s going to be one hell of a roller coaster ride.

\";\nwellstoneWinNarrow = \"

“A late, late projection on this unforgettable night…Paul Wellstone has just secured a nail-biting victory…”

When this campaign started, no one gave you a chance. After a bitterly fought primary that left many pro-Richards moderates feeling disaffected, with some even saying they would vote for Thompson, after everyone in the media wrote you off as being too far left, after all that, you could do nothing but wait and hope that your faith in America and the American people would be rewarded. When you finally retired to your HQ to watch the results with your closest advisors and your wife Sheila, you were restless, still feeling as though there was more to be done. You worried you hadn’t done enough. When most of the country had given up on finding out the results, you didn’t, you stayed up and waited, a lonely figure fighting for what had seemed like a hopeless cause.

Then the broadcast cut away on Tom Brokaw’s word, showing the map that had been burned into your memory. Your states were blue, Thomspon’s were red, and the electoral counter now had you past 270. Against all odds, you had stunned the pundits, the experts, maybe even yourself. You’d done it. From the son of humble Ukrainian Jewish immigrants to President of the United States, it’s a story that will inspire long after your time in government is over.

Historians will certainly be analyzing this election for years to come, not only for the unexpected outcome, but for what it means that the American people have entrusted the government to you. It seems like everything Gingrich said about this being a conservative country was proven to be propaganda after all. Three consecutive wins by a liberal have demonstrated that there is indeed a groundswell of progressivism in America; President Cuomo ignited that spark in 1992, and now you will carry it into the new millennium. What you can do with the flame that has been passed to you is uncertain.

Republicans still control the House, while Democrats have retained Senate control, helped by Jim Jeffords switching parties, so Dennis Hastert is going to do his damnedest to block all of our legislation, and you can expect gridlock for at least the next couple of years. You’ll probably have to cut some deals with the moderates to get things done. Let’s hope the midterms in ‘02 go better for us.

You receive a call of congratulations from President Cuomo, he’s as relieved as you are, and wishes you all the best. He will be a valuable counsel to you, much as you were to him. You watch the results for a while longer before finally going to bed. You’ve got a victory speech to prepare for tomorrow and a long four years ahead; if you play your cards right, it could become eight. Best of luck, Mr. Wellstone.

\";\nwellstoneWinStrong = \"

“This is the big one, it’s a result that no one expected at the start of this campaign, Paul Wellstone will become the 43rd President of the United States…”

When this campaign started, no one gave you a chance. After a bitterly fought primary that left many pro-Richards moderates feeling disaffected, with some even saying they would vote for Thompson, after everyone in the media wrote you off as being too far left, after all that, you might have been forgiven for throwing in the towel, but you never lost faith that the American people would connect with your progressive message. You always insisted that those early polls were underestimating you. When you finally retired to your HQ to watch the results with your closest advisors and your wife Sheila, you felt the satisfaction of knowing you had done all you could, and the rest was in Fate’s hands.

The early trends were going your way, and Tom Brokaw and Tim Russert began to seriously consider it. Then it happened, Brokaw’s decisive projection, followed by a display of the election map. Your states were blue, Thomspon’s were red, and it showed that you had not only won, but surpassed even your supporters’ expectations. Against all odds, you had stunned the pundits, the experts, maybe even yourself. You’d done it. From the son of humble Ukrainian Jewish immigrants to President of the United States, it’s a story that will inspire long after your time in government is over.

Historians will certainly be analyzing this election for years to come, not only for the unexpected outcome, but for what it means that the American people have entrusted the government to you in this sizable manner. It seems like everything Gingrich said about this being a conservative country was proven to be propaganda after all. Three consecutive wins by a liberal have demonstrated that there is indeed a groundswell of progressivism in America, a larger one that anyone thought; President Cuomo ignited that spark in 1992, and now you will carry it into the new millennium. What you do with the flame that has been passed to you depends on how well you can navigate Congress.

Democrats were able to narrow the GOP’s House majority to a handful of seats, so you’ll be hoping to get some of the moderate Republicans for work with you, at least in the first year, though Hastert will certainly try to block your every initiative. Meanwhile, Democrats have retained Senate control, helped by Jim Jeffords switching parties. Either way, expect gridlock and some intense negotiations over at least the next two years. Let’s hope the midterms in ‘02 go better for us.

You receive a call of congratulations from President Cuomo, he couldn’t be prouder, and wishes you all the best. He will be a valuable counsel to you, much as you were to him. You stand up, you’ve had a victory speech prepared, and now it looks like you’ll have a chance to use it. Enjoy the moment, sir, and get ready a long four years ahead; if you play your cards right, it could become eight. Best of luck, Mr. Wellstone.

\";\nwellstoneWinCommanding = \"

“Paul Wellstone: A Man of the People”

You are at your campaign HQ watching the results pour in when your wife Sheila hands you a paper and points you to a column with this title. The piece was written by legendary Minnesota journalist Jim Klobuchar and published on the morning of Election Day, neither as a proclamation of victory or defeat, but as a profile of the man himself.

And yet, with the decisive results you’re watching unfold now, the whole thing feels almost prophetic. It details the life and times of one Paul David Wellstone, adopted son of Minnesota, a former teacher devoted to his students, a current Senator, and soon, the 43rd President of the United States. It speaks of your humble upbringing as the son of Ukrainian Jewish immigrants, of your lifelong fight for the causes of labor and justice. It speaks of you as an icon within the progressive movement, and the heir to President Cuomo in the eyes of many. Now, you have fulfilled that dream, and you’ve done it in a way that can leave no doubt that America is ready to take its first strides in the new millennium with a progressive visionary at the helm.

As you step out to give your victory speech, your supporters greet you with wild cheers and applause, for you will continue the lineage of FDR and LBJ. That which President Cuomo carried for eight years, he will now pass to you, as the inheritor of his legacy. It is now up to you to be a faithful steward and guide this country into the great unknown that is the 21st century. The people have spoken, and they have given you a mandate to continue the work of the 1990s and build upon it as you see fit. Perhaps you will tackle corruption in the political system, or finally realize your dream to move America to a single payer healthcare system.

Whatever you do, you’ll have at least two years to do it. Democrats have not only increased their Senate majority, with Jim Jeffords’ party switch just being the icing on the cake, but have also retaken the House just two years after losing it. Deep down, you know that despite the euphoria you feel now, the fight is far from over. The establishment will fight you at every turn, the moderates in Congress will make a fuss over your agenda. But you will navigate these challenges as you have everything else, with courage and compassion.

After three straight victories by a liberal candidate, analysts and pundits are scrambling to determine the cause of this shift. Many are still puzzled by how you managed to reverse Reagan’s campaign against “the L word”, but suddenly liberalism seems to be en vogue again, much like during the golden age post-WWII. You receive a call of congratulations from President Cuomo, he couldn’t be prouder, of course. He will be a valuable counsel to you, much as you were to him. You set the paper down and take Sheila’s hand as you two sit comfortably and watch Brokaw and Russert talk about what this means for America. Everything else can wait till tomorrow. Tonight, you are on top of the world.

\";\nwellstoneWinLand = \"

“The New Liberal Century”

(The following is an excerpt from the book “Paul Wellstone: The Quest for the Second Bill of Rights”, published in the year 2032)

President Wellstone was often fond of saying that the only way America was going to shake off its corrupt political system was by uniting and delivering a clear message to corporate donors that the people’s voices would not be silenced. As an example of just such a moment, he always pointed back to his own election in 2000, a truly transformative moment in American politics. Wellstone, then a Senator from Minnesota, had entered the race as an underdog after a tough primary contest, and many experts gave him very little chance to win.

However, despite being given such long odds, Wellstone was able to hold on to the Cuomo coalition - something that many had predicted he would not be able to do - and won a resounding victory, the third such impressive margin in a row for Democrats.

The election was, with hindsight, a significant milestone in the political landscape of this country, for it seemingly swept away any remaining doubts about whether the liberalism of FDR and Cuomo could survive in this new and changing world. In his first term, President Wellstone and the Democratic Congress put campaign finance reform at the top of the agenda, passing legislation to limit the influence of corporations in political campaigns. He also became a champion of renewable energy, a position that started to gain traction even with moderate Republicans.

By his second term, President Wellstone was ready to take his reforms to another level. He announced his intention to revive FDR’s Second Bill of Rights, updated for modern times. This policy initiative (sometimes informally known as the “New New Deal”). The first major legislation to be passed under this initiative in 2005 was Wellstone’s long cherished dream, a bill codifying single-payer healthcare into law.

Wellstone was able to focus on his domestic agenda due to the government successfully eliminating the terrorist Osama bin Laden in a raid on July 25th, 2001, just a few months into Wellstone's first term. The government focusing its efforts on limiting the effects of terrorism rather than funding direct military intervention has been credited with the tremendous progress of the 2000s, which, together with the 1990s, represent the Second Golden Age of liberalism. Mr. Wellstone is far from a spring chicken at 88 years old, but he still intends to vote in this year’s election, and to do his part to maintain the Liberal Century that he helped to build…

\";\nwellstoneLossClose = \"

“Senator Wellstone surprised a lot of people, Charlie, but it just wasn’t quite enough…”

You went to sleep last night uncertain of your future. The race had been a toss up for weeks, and the media had been caught completely off guard by you steadily closing the gap on Thomspon, who seemed to have all the advantages early on, given your outspoken progressivism, which the pundits had all predicted would be your downfall. Even when the polls showed the race tightening, many still dismissed you. Despite this, you pressed on, powered by nothing by raw conviction. You could almost reach out and touch victory.

Early the next morning, you turned on the TV and were greeted by this message from the Good Morning America team of Charlie Gibson and Diane Sawyer. It felt surreal to find out this way, the same way that many people who didn’t stay up were probably finding out. And yet there was something tragically poetic about the whole thing. Throughout your career as a teacher and Senator, you had always taken pride in being a man of, by and for the people, and now you had learned your fate in about the most ordinary way possible. Fred Thompson had eked it out, only narrowly, but by enough. The leadership of the nation would fall on his shoulders.

You keep watching as Diane and Charlie talk to some analysts and interview some voters from both sides. The race was one of the closest in living memory, a true battle where every state and every vote counted. Despite Cuomo leaving office with a good economy and some landmark achievements, you still had a mountain to climb due to the nation seemingly tiring of big government liberalism and preparing to swing back to the right. You were an underdog in the primaries to begin with, and uniting the party was seen as too tall of a task, let alone uniting the country.

Yet, you never allowed these tremendous challenges to slow you down or give you pause. You fought bravely until the very end, but maybe the pundits were right after all, maybe your ideas were just a bit ahead of their time. Maybe America just wasn’t ready for Paul Wellstone. Or maybe..the thought haunts you, maybe you just weren’t good enough. Maybe you threw away a winnable election. You feel a hand on your shoulder; you know right away that it’s your wife, Sheila. She always seems to know when you’re being too tough on yourself, and she always manages to make things better. You’re going to need her now more than ever.

You keep watching the show as Diane and Charlie talk about what Thomspon’s election might mean for America. One thing that’s clear is that divided government will continue to reign in Washington, with Republicans holding the House and Democrats holding the Senate, thanks partly to Jim Jeffords’ defection. Hopefully, the Senate can put a check on the hard right, and the new President will uphold his promise to be a uniter rather than tearing down everything President Cuomo built. You, meanwhile, will return to the Senate and continue your fight for a fairer American system, and your 2000 campaign will hopefully inspire another progressive to take up the mantle in four years time. For now, prepare to give one final speech to your heartbroken, but still adoring supporters.

\";\nwellstoneLossNarrow = \"

“In one of the closest Presidential elections of our time, we can at last project that Fred Thompson has crossed 270 electoral votes…”

It was late in the night, and you were sitting alone in your campaign HQ, watching the TV screen where Tom Brokaw had just made his projection. At the start of campaign season, many of the pundits had insisted that you were too liberal for the electorate, that your hopes of overcoming Thompson’s lead were hopeless, and that the race might as well have been called after the convention, but you never allowed that to slow you down. You ran an inspired campaign, fighting back against all the doubters, and closed the gap until the self-appointed experts had no choice to admit that the unthinkable might happen.

Now, as you see the map showing Thompson has crossed the 270 mark, as you hear Brokaw and Tim Russert discuss exactly what this means for the country, you feel a profound sense of melancholy. After all of your efforts, you’ve come this close only to fall agonizingly short. You sigh to yourself and reflect on every moment that led up to this point. You think about all the decisions you made and wonder what you could have done differently. You wonder…you wonder if maybe Richards would have won.

In the end, perhaps America just wasn’t quite ready for another outspoken liberal such as yourself. You had hoped that after 8 years of President Cuomo’s leadership, America would finally break free from the Reagan era brainwashing against liberalism, and tonight did show that the conservatives had severely underestimated your strength. You were able to get a lot more support than expected, but the polarization in America has seemingly ended President Cuomo’s hopes of reviving the old New Deal coalition. While you were able to mobilize progressives and even win over some moderates, the nation seemed to be ready to move on from the liberalism of the Cuomo years.

You call Fred Thompson to concede. He is gracious and wishes you well. You hope that he will live up to his promises to be a unifying president and push back against the Far Right’s attempts to dismantle everything you’ve worked for over the last decade. Republicans, as expected, have maintained their House majority, but all is not lost, as Democrats still control the Senate, partially thanks to Jim Jeffords switching parties, so we will at least be able to put a check on Hastert and his bunch. Hopefully, we can make more gains in the 2002 Midterms.

You will run for re-election to the Senate then, if you so choose. You are still beloved in your home state of Minnesota, and it is not expected that you will be given a serious challenge. While you fell short in this election, you still shocked a lot of people, and you hold out hope that it will someday inspire someone else to carry on the fight. Perhaps, just as you had Walter, you will become a mentor figure for the next rising star of Minnesota politics. And the narrowness of the result gives you some comfort in knowing that progress may one day prevail.

You glance at the door and see Sheila, your wife, standing there. She stayed up after all, worrying about you, as always. You stand up and turn the TV off, you’ve seen all you need to. You take her arm and the two of you walk away. Away from the election of 2000 and into the next chapter of your life.

\";\nwellstoneLossStrong = \"

“And now, ladies and gentlemen, a major projection: Fed Thomspon has just been elected the next President of the United States...”

You sit in your campaign HQ with your staffers and family, watching the TV screen where Tom Brokaw has just made his projection. You had begun the day knowing the polls were putting you in a bad position, but still convinced that somehow, you could overcome the odds and shock the world again. Even when you’d seen articles in the news, seen the talking heads on TV discussing the uphill battle you faced, even when they insisted that you were too liberal for the electorate, that your hopes of overcoming Thompson’s lead were diminishing, you never allowed that to slow you down. You had exhausted every possible resource, every speech, every campaign stop.

But now, as you see the map showing Thompson has crossed the 270 mark, as you hear Brokaw and Tim Russert discuss exactly what this means for the country, you feel a deep sense of disappointment, you feel as though you’ve let everybody down. You receive some consolatory hugs and words from your staffers, they’ve worked long and hard on this campaign, and you’re grateful to them. Your wife Sheila is also there to take your hand and assure you that you did all you could.

In the end, perhaps America just wasn’t ready for another outspoken liberal such as yourself. You had hoped that after 8 years of President Cuomo’s leadership, America would finally break free from the Reagan era brainwashing against liberalism, but tonight has proved that even after all the progress made, people simply couldn’t connect with your message. Perhaps President Cuomo’s election was an anomaly, a example of being in the right place at the right time, rather than a true shift back to left wing policies becoming mainstream again. You believed so deeply in his message, in his ideas, yet it seems like so many of your fellow Americans were just ready to move on.

You call Fred Thompson to concede. He is gracious and wishes you well. You hope that he will live up to his promises to be a unifying president and push back against the Far Right’s attempts to dismantle everything you’ve worked for over the last decade. It will be a tough battle to do so, as Republicans expanded their House majority, but all is not lost, as Democrats still control the Senate, thanks to Jim Jeffords switching parties, so we will at least be able to put a check on Hastert and his bunch. Hopefully, we can make more gains in the 2002 Midterms.

You will run for re-election to the Senate then, if you so choose. You are still beloved in your home state of Minnesota, and it is not expected that you will be given a serious challenge. Your run ended the way many pundits predicted, well short of victory, and yet, you hold out hope that it will someday inspire someone else to carry on the fight.

Perhaps, just as you had Walter, you will become a mentor figure for the next rising star of Minnesota politics. While tonight was a setback, you can at least take comfort in knowing that progress may one day prevail. You leave the room with Sheila, ignoring the TV still playing in the background, you’ve seen all you need to. You take her arm and the two of you walk away. Away from the election of 2000 and into the next chapter of your life.

\";\nwellstoneLossLarge = \"

“While polling remains open in the west, we are confident in projecting that Fred Thompson will win the presidency tonight…”

You sit in your campaign HQ silently, staring at the TV screen where Tom Brokaw has just made that projection. It seemed like the night had only just begun, but it was already over. Truthfully, many had known that this was the most likely outcome for weeks. Everyone in the media had been saying it, and even you, as much as you hated to admit it, had to admit in your heart and soul at a certain point that it was no longer about winning, but about remaining dignified.

So you held your head up and pushed onwards through everything that was hurled at you. The Right had picked your campaign apart from the beginning, calling you a radical leftist, and for whatever reason, you could never get out from the shadow of those attacks. Even some Democrats had abandoned you, turning on their own with an “I told you so” haughtiness, claiming that Richards never would’ve lost like this. You hate to admit it, but maybe…maybe they’re right.

Maybe your ideas really were just too far out there for people to accept. You had hoped that after 8 years of President Cuomo’s leadership, America would finally break free from the Reagan era brainwashing against liberalism, but tonight has proved that it was simply too much for you to overcome. Perhaps President Cuomo’s election was an anomaly, a example of being in the right place at the right time, rather than a true shift back to left wing policies becoming mainstream again. You believed so deeply in his message, in his ideas, yet it seems like so many of your fellow Americans were just ready to move on.

You call Fred Thompson to concede. He is gracious and wishes you well. You hope that he will live up to his promises to be a unifying president and push back against the Far Right’s attempts to dismantle everything you’ve worked for over the last decade. Unfortunately, those Far Right voices will be stronger than ever, as not only have the Republicans expanded their House majority, but they have also taken control of the Senate, so Democrats will have very little in the way of means to fight off Hastert’s agenda. Hopefully, we can make up for this in the 2002 Midterms.

You will run for re-election to the Senate then, if you so choose. You are still beloved in your home state of Minnesota, and it is not expected that you will be given a serious challenge. In the end, you have turned up quite similarly to your friend and mentor, Walter Mondale. Beaten decisively in a presidential election, and yet, you hold out hope that your run will someday inspire someone else to carry on the fight. Perhaps, just as you had Walter, you will become a mentor figure for the next rising star of Minnesota politics. That is the best you can hope for now, and that is what will drive you as you seek to leave behind the bitter disappointment of tonight.

You turn off the TV, you’ve seen all you need to. You stand up and head to the door, where your wife Sheila is waiting. You take her arm and the two of you walk away. Away from the election of 2000 and into the next chapter of your life.

\";\nwellstoneLossLand = \"

“Farewell To a Dream.”

(The following is an excerpt from a memoir published in 2028 with the above title, written by a campaign staffer from Mr. Wellstone’s failed 2000 presidential run)

If the people of this country believed in Paul Wellstone’s ideals even a fraction as much as he did, perhaps he would have been President. A very fine President, if you ask me, though I confess my bias up front. Mr. Wellstone was a lion of a man. He didn’t look it, but if you pushed his buttons on an issue he held dear, my goodness, would he let you have it. His convictions, his sense of moral character, wouldn’t allow him to settle, it was one of his greatest qualities, but also his greatest flaw as a politician. Perhaps that was why 2000 went the way that it did. All of us on the team believed so strongly in him and his message, that maybe we just lost sight of the rest of the country.

Mr. Wellstone - it feels wrong to call him Paul, even now - I can still remember Election Night, he gathered us all up at the HQ and was very forthright, “We’re not going to win,” he said, I remember that clear as day. And we were all shocked, of course. “What do you mean, we’re not going to win?” We must’ve thought. We didn’t understand. Oh sure, we’d seen the polling, but it just didn’t sink in until then. Not until Mr. Wellstone told us.

But I remember what he said next. He said “This is not farewell to the dream. It's just going to take a bit longer to finish what we started.” I’m sure I’m not the only one who has carried those words with me. I’ve never been ashamed to say I worked on the Wellstone 2000 campaign, because no matter how lopsided the result, I never gave up on that dream. As I look at our politics now, I see so many of Mr. Wellstone’s ideas, the things they called radical back then, now are perfectly mainstream. I think if he were here with us now, he would be proud of how far we’ve come, but he would also urge us on to even greater heights. I can’t think of any better way to honor Mr. Wellstone’s legacy.

The South feels that you’ve sold your soul to the national party, they just don’t get it. You certainly do your best to embrace modern, trendy campaigning. Indeed, some people do like the change, but many others miss the old Ann Richards." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 90047, "fields": { "answer": 80047, "candidate": 78, "answer_feedback": "It’s not an easy balance to strike, Ma’am. People notice that you seem a bit more restrained, but they just accept it. You could come close to Carter’s margins in ‘76 at this rate. Progressives, however, are deeply frustrated with you and some are even considering voting Reform in protest." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 90051, "fields": { "answer": 80051, "candidate": 78, "answer_feedback": "A pretty good middle course to take, Madam VP, especially if you want to reap the benefits of Cuomo’s most popular policies while leaving yourself some wiggle room to stake out your own positions at some point down the road. After all, it’s your name on the ticket." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 90052, "fields": { "answer": 80052, "candidate": 78, "answer_feedback": "Ultimately, staying true to yourself is probably for the best. The sorts of people who would not vote for you on the basis on sex are the sort who would vote for a wet paper bag over a Democrat. Of course, it won’t make everyone happy, but it definitely combats a lot of the sexism being hurled at you by the right and draws in more moderate support." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 90054, "fields": { "answer": 80054, "candidate": 78, "answer_feedback": "You take your advisors’ word for it. America just isn’t ready for a woman running for President to fully embrace her femininity. The ads play well in the South and other more socially moderate to conservative regions. Let’s hope you can find a way to get them back on your side…" } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 90055, "fields": { "answer": 80055, "candidate": 78, "answer_feedback": "This is a bold stance, Madam VP, and one that once again cements you in the minds of your female supporters as one of the great women of the century.
